title: Metis
text:
Metis is directly a cunning intelligence or being a skilled manipluator, not being inherently good or bad, but is often perverted to manipulate and deceive others in a harmful way. This type of deceitful rhetoric often involves using persuassion, ethos, and manipulative language to achieve a desired outcome, often overlooking truth or ethics.






My analyis will be grounded within three theoriests and their respective theories.

Michel Foucault’s theories of Light/Visibilty vs. a Hidden
Deleuze and Guattari’s theory of Nomadology
The Theories of Deceptive Rhetoric and Metis



Foucault looks at the relationship between Light (Visibility) and a Hidden, placing the conversation within the context of power. He works to remove the idea away from the traditional notion that light and visibility are representative of a truth or freedom, instead looking at how light and visibility become a tool for insitutional illumination for discipline and subjugation. Visibility is no longer a privelage; it is now a vulnerability.

title: ContentOps
text:
Content Operations (ContentOps) is the framework that aligns people and technology to produce, manage, and distribute content. ContentOps looks at the system in place for content creation, rather than looking at the content itself as individual acts of craft. The entirety of ContentOps looks to understand that creators are supported by workflows and technical infastracture to limit bottlenecking, ensuring that content creation is not an isolated or singular event.



Within athletics, and specifically collegiate football, there is a necessity for an outpouring of highquality and constant content. The media cycle for college athletics is often a never-ending and relentless process where content must be produce and distributed at a consistently high-volume and high-quality. ContentOps is the engine behind institutional control of narratives within the athletic department. The rapid flow of content allows for a projection of institutional stability and identity, allowing a program to use content strategy to deploy a unified message and identity, reacting in real-time to events on and off the field.



Collegiate football programs have recently crafted an interesting landscape. The manner in which an athletic department will completely change its own identity to fit that of their head football coach and, just as quickly, change said identity immediately upon that coaches departure reveals a tension between coaching mobility and institutional loyalty worth analyzing. Coaches often preach messages of “loyalty” and “brotherhood” but are quick to leave when a more lucrative opportunity presents itself, taking the identity of the program with them. These identity shifts exist in a seemingly never-ending game of tug-of-war, attempting to maintain some balance on the core values of the institution while still reflecting the head of their program. This identity tension is the direct result of a ContentOps strategy that is forced to constantly produce content with the goal of maintaining institutional identity (and control) but has to reinvent itself to a fanbase everytime a coach leaves. This apparatus, then, will reveal the rhetorical strategies that institutions attempt to use to maintain power within a landscape that provides little certainty.

title: Metis and Theory
text:
Metis is directly a cunning intelligence or being a skilled manipluator, not being inherently good or bad, but is often perverted to manipulate and deceive others in a harmful way. This type of deceitful rhetoric often involves using persuassion, ethos, and manipulative language to achieve a desired outcome, often overlooking truth or ethics.






My analyis will be grounded within three theoriests and their respective theories.

Michel Foucault’s theories of Light/Visibilty vs. a Hidden
Deleuze and Guattari’s theory of Nomadology
The Theories of Deceptive Rhetoric and Metis



Foucault looks at the relationship between Light (Visibility) and a Hidden, placing the conversation within the context of power. He works to remove the idea away from the traditional notion that light and visibility are representative of a truth or freedom, instead looking at how light and visibility become a tool for insitutional illumination for discipline and subjugation. Visibility is no longer a privelage; it is now a vulnerability.
Working from Jeremy Bentham’s Panopticon, Foucault examines how prisioners are placed under a constant gaze within a circular prison, light streaming into their space and bodies, rendering them visibile at all times. This idea of the panopticon reveals the idea that the subject is always in the light but is unable to see the hidden observer, creating an assumption of constant surveillance, forcing the observed to self-regulate their behavior, policing themselves.
Foucault will then look to the medical field, examining how the clinical gaze penetrates the flesh, turning a subjective experience of sickness into an objective case for examination. Here, light becomes the mechanism for extraction, forcing hidden aspects of existence, like disease and madness, into a visible state where they can be categorized and controlled, where being seen is being made an object of knowledge.
Shifting towards discourse, Foucault argues that power structures create a demand for visibility, where the subject is forced to bring their hidden life into light of language. Power, in this way, does not operate by repressing the hidden, rather it demands that the hidden be spoken and revealed. Once those hidden desires or thoughts are illuminated through discourse, they can be regulated and normalized by insitutional power.
There is power, then, in remaining hidden. Institutions hide the mechanisms of their power while demanding transparency and visibility from their subjects. When the subject navigates institutional spaces, their visibility leaves them vulnerable for discipline and normalization. Instutions use visibilty as a tool that manipulates a vulnerable subject while concealing their own mechanisms of power, hiding behind a percieved veil of transparency.
This framework provides a basis for understanding how modern institutions, like universities and colleges, control subjects, not through physical chains of bondage, but by managing what is visible and what is allowed to remain hidden.

title: Case Studies
text:
This research aims to examine three specific case studies of coaches that departed from an institution looking specifically at the rhetoric surrounding each coach prior to their departure and arrival at each institution

  



Deion Sanders is well known by fans and non-fans alike. His name is synonymous with flash and football. Deion’s first collegiate head coaching job was in 2020 being hired by Jackson State University, a notable HBCU. During his tenure as the head coach of the tigers, much of the rhetoric that surrounded the team was of transforming the narrative that HBCU’s could not put together a notable football program, that they could not land the big recruits, that these schools were valuable to the black community and could compete with the blue-blood programs around the country. The messaging was clear. Deion aimed to transform the program, crafting a new identity for the storied institution.
Problems arise in 2022 when Coach Sanders decided to leave the program after two seasons accepting the head coaching job at the University of Colorado, taking the recruits and identity with him. Prior to his arrival, Jackson State had built a ContentOps strategy centered around “Brotherhood” and HBCU Pride. This identity was subjugated by Deion’s personal brand, with the institution embracing the “Coach Prime” persona, placing national attention on the university. There was an attempt by the institution to place labor and fan capital in a fixed position, however this position was overturned with Sander’s acting at the Deleuzian “Nomad,” using Jackson State’s own content apparatus to accumulate more social capital before leaving to Colorado, leaving little behind in terms of identity and culture.


This change in ContentOps is not exclusive to the left institution either. The University of Colorado

Deleuze and Guattari’s theory of Nomadology is driven by the interactions between two entities; the war machine and the state. The “State” does not refer specifically to the government, but rather is the rigid institutions that capture, organize, measure, and enclose, establishing rigid borders that demand loyalty and make everything permenant and predictable. The “War Machine” is not literal, working as a figurative force of pure exteriority and destruction. The nomad is the operator of the war machine, breaking down the walls that are constructed by the state. Within this theory, the nomad is distinctly mobile, refusing to be fixed or defined by the state’s definitions. If the nomad is embraced by the state, they either disrupt the institution from within or slip away.



Metis and Deceptive Rhetoric have already been touched upon within this page, however, there is more nuance to consider. Within modern rhetorical studies, Metis is analyzed more as a way to subvert dominant power structures. When rigid institutional spaces are navigated, deceptive rhetoric and Metis is used as a form of survival, giving the institutions what they want to hear but cloaking the true intentions of the agent navigating that space. This allows a maintenance of leverage where agents can hide their true intentions and slip away before they can be captured. Both Metis and Deceptive Rhetoric work to subvert institutional power, providing a survivability for those navigating institutions that hide their own mechanisms, evening the power imbalance.
